goal: Open the compelling question with a state commuting table, sort variables as categorical or quantitative, and build frequency and relative frequency tables.

goal: Describe the distribution of a categorical variable with bar charts and relative frequencies, and name its level of measurement, in first-year college vocabulary.

goal: Read joint, marginal and conditional distributions from a two-way table of commuting mode by state, and draw a segmented bar chart.

Model reactivated: two-way-table, one familiar table first. Data: US Census Bureau community survey tables of how workers get to work and commute times, by state (data.census.gov, as of the survey year). Sensitivity (income and identity): tables by state, never by group; no student shares their own commute or home location.

goal: Decide whether two categorical variables are associated in a new two-way table (commuting mode by travel-time band in one state) and argue it from conditional distributions.
note: Ours. Data: US Census Bureau community survey tables of how workers get to work and commute times, by state (data.census.gov, as of the survey year). Sensitivity (income and identity): tables by state, never by group; no student shares their own commute or home location.

goal: Display a quantitative distribution with a dot plot, a stemplot and a histogram, and describe its shape, center, spread and unusual values in context.
note: Base OS 2.1 (stemplots) and OS 2.2 (histograms). Review day 1 of 2.5 for displays and summaries (50 minutes toward the cap). Retrieval task (10 minutes, practice, never check evidence; a student who misses it gets a brief reminder with the earlier model): alg1-data-displays (dot plots, histograms and box plots from Algebra I). goal: Find the mean, median, quartiles, interquartile range and standard deviation of a data set, by hand for a small set and with the calculator for a large one, and say what each measures.

Retrieval task (10 minutes, practice, never check evidence; a student who misses it gets a brief reminder with the earlier model): alg1-center-spread (comparing center and spread). Data: one station's daily high temperatures for one year (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, National Centers for Environmental Information daily summaries, as of the year).

goal: Draw a box plot by hand from a five-number summary, flag outliers with the 1.5 times IQR rule, and choose resistant or non-resistant summaries to fit the shape.
note: Base OS 2.4 and OS 2.6. Model reactivated: box-plot, drawn by hand before technology. Data: national park visits and daily highs (unit 1 sources).

goal: Practice summarizing distributions with the calculator: five-number summaries, means and standard deviations, box plots and outlier checks on new data cards.
note: Base OS 2.8 lab with supplied data (park visits; the base survey of shoes owned is cut). The half review day of displays and summaries (25 minutes toward the cap); the rest is practice of days 5 to 7. A second skewed set summarized two ways is an extension only. Named fluency CUR-ST.2: kept in the daily opening for the rest of the year, untimed.

goal: Compare two or more distributions in context (commute times in two states, or daily highs in two seasons) by shape, center, spread and outliers, with displays side by side.

tools: dot-plot; box-plot; statistics applet (device per pair)

goal: Locate a value in a distribution with a percentile and a z-score, and compare values from different distributions by their z-scores.
note: Base OS 2.3 (percentiles) and OS 2.7 (z-scores). Data: daily highs at two stations (unit 1 source).

goal: Show what adding a constant and multiplying by a constant do to the center, spread and shape of a distribution, converting daily highs from Fahrenheit to Celsius.

goal: Read a density curve as area, then fit a normal model with its mean and standard deviation and estimate areas with the 68-95-99.7 rule.

goal: Practice z-scores, percentiles and normal areas and cut-offs with the table on new contexts, each with a sketch of the curve.

goal: Build the correlation coefficient from standardized values, read its sign and size, and explain why a strong correlation still does not show cause.

note: Base OS 12.2 (formulas) and OS 12.4 (prediction). Data: vehicle weight against miles per gallon (US Department of Energy and Environmental Protection Agency fuel economy data, one model year, as of that year); vehicle classes only, makes and models removed.

goal: Practice fitting and interpreting least-squares lines, r and r squared with the calculator on new data, and judge each prediction.
note: Base OS 12.7 textbook cost lab, with its published prices (product names removed). Data: OpenStax, Statistics, lab data (as published).

goal: Analyze the full fuel economy data set: fit, interpret and predict, and write what the line can and cannot tell a buyer.

goal: Read a residual plot, and tell outliers, high-leverage points and influential points by their effect on the line.
note: Base OS 12.5 and Lane 14 (influential observations). Data: vehicle weight against miles per gallon (US Department of Energy and Environmental Protection Agency fuel economy data, one model year, as of that year); vehicle classes only, makes and models removed.

goal: Straighten a curved relationship with a logarithm: the US census counts 1790 to 1900, fitted on the log scale and turned back into an exponential curve.

goal: Straighten a curve with a square root or a reciprocal, choosing by the residual plot: speeds and stopping distances of 1920s cars.
note: Base Lane 16 (the ladder of powers). Data: speeds and stopping distances as published by Ezekiel (1930).

goal: Fit a transformed model to a new data set, turn the fitted line back into a curve, predict with it, and check the residual plot of the transformed fit.
note: Base Lane 16 (ladder of powers, worked problems). A power model on log-log axes is an extension only.

goal: Model the yearly mean carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa: fit a line, read the residual plot's curve, and choose and defend a better model.
note: Ours. Data: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, Global Monitoring Laboratory, Mauna Loa yearly means (as of the year read). goal: End-of-unit assessment: one sitting of unseen items on new data, with a prompt for each part of CUR-ST.4 (least squares, slope and intercept in context, formulas from summaries, r and r squared, prediction and extrapolation) and CUR-ST.5 (residual plots, outliers, leverage and influence, a transformation fitted and turned back).

goal: Act on the end-of-unit results: regroup by the items missed, repair with the earlier model, and redo one item per code.

goal: Name the kinds of bias (undercoverage, nonresponse, wording, voluntary response, convenience) and say which way each pushes an estimate.

goal: Critique the sampling plans of three published surveys and design a sampling plan for a new question, naming the likely bias of each choice.
note: Ours. Surveys on neutral public topics (park use, commuting).

goal: Tell an experiment from an observational study, and name the principles of a good experiment: comparison, random assignment and replication, with confounding as the reason.
note: Base OS 1.4 and Lane 6 (causation). Retrieval task (10 minutes, practice, never check evidence; a student who misses it gets a brief reminder with the earlier model): alg2-experiments-significance (comparing two treatments by re-randomizing, Algebra II unit 7).

goal: Read the polio vaccine field trial's two designs side by side and explain what the placebo, blinding and random assignment of the one half gave that the observed-control half could not.
note: Base OS 1.4 (ethics). Data: the 1954 polio vaccine field trial from its published summary report (Francis and colleagues, 1955) and later public accounts. Sensitivity (health): the trial is told with its history, and the children and families in it as people; no student shares any health data.

goal: Design experiments with blocking and with matched pairs, and explain why each removes a source of variation.
note: Base Lane 6 (experimental designs). The matched-pairs design here is the one unit 8 analyzes. A blocked paper-helicopter experiment is an extension only.

goal: State the scope of inference of a study from how it was done: random sampling lets us generalize, random assignment lets us conclude cause, and each case of the two-by-two grid.
note: Base Lane 6 (causation), second part.

goal: Redesign Biology's feedback-mechanism investigation on paper as a randomized experiment, with treatments, assignment, blocking if fitting, and its scope of inference.
note: Ours. Calls back to Biology (science HS-LS1-3, bio-homeostasis-feedback, grade 9); the design is taught here. Sensitivity (health): on paper only; no student measures or shares a heart rate or any health data.

goal: Judge study reports from the news: name the design, the likely bias or confounding, and what the study lets us conclude.
note: Ours. Reports on neutral topics (study habits, plant growth, park use).

goal: End-of-unit assessment: one sitting of unseen items, with a prompt for each part of CUR-ST.6 (the four sample designs drawn, the five kinds of bias and their effect) and CUR-ST.7 (comparison, random assignment, replication, blocking, matched pairs, placebo and blinding, experiment or observational study, scope of inference).
note: Ours. Every study and data set is new to the student. Response on day 43.

goal: Act on the end-of-unit results: regroup by the items missed, repair with a worked design, and redo one item per code.
note: Ours. The response to day 42, counted once.

goal: Pose a statistical question for the investigation and draft a data collection plan of one of the two kinds (a randomized experiment within the class or a random sample from a public data set), using unit 3's designs.

goal: Revise the data collection plan with the teacher's written feedback and have it approved, with its scope of inference stated.
note: Base OS 1.5 lab, second part. Held day 2. No data is gathered before approval. Sensitivity: questions avoid sensitive personal data; any class data is anonymous, voluntary and harmless (recall of a list, estimating a 30-second interval, letters in a word), and students never measure or share their bodies.

goal: Open the compelling question with the shared-birthday puzzle, and find probabilities by simulation with dice and cards, seeing the law of large numbers in pooled class results.

goal: Use the complement and addition rules, and tell mutually exclusive events from independent ones, in first-year college notation.

goal: Find conditional probabilities from two-way tables, apply the general multiplication rule, and test independence.

Genetics crosses use pea plants and fruit flies, never a student's family traits; ratios are expected values from theory, not data. goal: Count outcomes with the multiplication principle and permutations, and use counts to find probabilities.

goal: Solve the shared-birthday problem by the complement and by simulation, then a set of new compound problems, choosing rules or counting for each.

note: Ours. Response on day 57.
